record.filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
record.stem: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US
record.central_claim: The risk of 1970s-style stagflation in the US is overblown because the high debt-to-GDP ratio prevents the Fed from raising rates as in the 1970s, and alternative policies like bank deregulation could foster production that reduces inflation and debt.

arguments.conclusion: The 1970s stagflation was characterized by rising inflation and unemployment, volatile GDP growth, and was ultimately ended by Volcker's high interest rates.
premises: Inflation peaked at 12.4% in 1980 and rose in multiple waves from 1965.
GDP growth was volatile, with negative growth in 1974-75 and 1980-82.
Unemployment rose until peaking in 1982.
Fed funds rate peaked at 20% in 1981 to crush inflation.

evidence.item: CPI rose from 1.2% in 1965 to peaks of 6.3% in 1970, 9.1% in 1975, and 12.4% in 1980.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: 1965 inflation was reading at 1.2% rose before it peaked in 1970 at 6.3% ... rose again to a peak of 9.1% in 1975 ... peaked for the last time at 12.4% in 1980

evidence.item: GDP growth dipped to 0.2% in 1970 and had negative growth in 1974-75 and 1980-82.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: GDP was well above 5% and then dipped to a bottom of 0.2% in 1970 ... declining GDP in 74 and 75 ... dipped below to negative growth again in 1980 and in 1982

evidence.item: Unemployment rose until peaking in 1982.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: unemployment was dropping until about 1969, and then it started rising before it peaked in 1982

evidence.item: Fed funds rate peaked at almost 20% in 1981.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: they hiked it finally to a peak of almost 20% in 1981

themes.theme: Current constraints due to high US debt-to-GDP ratio

arguments.conclusion: The high debt-to-GDP ratio prevents the Fed from raising interest rates as Volcker did because the government cannot afford the debt service costs.
premises: Current debt-to-GDP ratio is above 120%.
Post-WWII debt-to-GDP was above 120% but was reduced to 30% by various means.
If interest rates rose significantly, interest on national debt would go to $2-$3 trillion or more.
The government currently cannot make minimum payments and must borrow more.

evidence.item: Debt-to-GDP post-WWII was above 120%, fell to around 30%.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: The debt-to-GDP ratio following World War II was up above 120% ... and it bottomed around 30%

evidence.item: Current debt-to-GDP is above 120%.
evidence.verification_basis: Transcript asserts current ratio but does not provide a source or exact recent figure.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: right now with the Fed funds rate sitting under 4%, you do not have the ability for the Fed to do the same thing ... when your debt is above 120%

evidence.item: Interest alone on national debt would go to $2 trillion, $3 trillion or more.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: Just the interest alone on the national debt would go to $2 trillion, $3 trillion, or way more if the Federal Reserve tried to do anything close to what they did in the '70s

evidence.item: The US government right now can't even make their minimum payments. They have to borrow more from a new credit card.
evidence.verification_basis: Strong fiscal claim with no supporting data or source.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: the US government right now can't even make their minimum payments. They have to borrow more from a new credit card just to make their minimum payments

analogies.explanation: Illustrates that with low debt-to-income, rate hikes are manageable, but with high debt-to-income, even modest rate increases can bankrupt.
analogies.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
analogies.source_excerpt: It'd be like if you made a hundred grand a year and you had $30,000 worth of debt... if you make a hundred grand a year and you owe $120,000 in debt, even a modest increase in the interest rate might bankrupt you

themes.theme: Money supply growth versus oil price shocks

arguments.conclusion: Oil shocks do not cause sustained broad inflation without money supply growth; they redirect purchasing power.
premises: Inflation is largely driven by money supply outpacing production.
2020-2021 money supply increased 25%, causing inflation.
Money supply is not increasing massively recently.
An oil shock is like a rent doubling: you cut other spending, not all prices rise.

evidence.item: Money supply increased by a record 25% in 2020 and 2021.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: they increased the money supply by a record 25% in 2020 and 2021

evidence.item: Money supply is increasing again but no massive increase recently.
evidence.verification_basis: No data or timeframe provided to verify recent growth rate.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: the money supply is increasing, but there is no massive increase happening recently that is any different than what's been going on for the last couple of years

evidence.item: During the Great Financial Crisis, money supply did not increase much because they printed base money but not overall money supply.
evidence.verification_basis: Explanation offered but no numeric comparison or source.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: Even though they did a lot of money printing, it didn't result in the overall money supply increasing

analogies.explanation: Shows that a single price increase forces consumers to cut other spending, preventing broad inflation without money growth.
analogies.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
analogies.source_excerpt: For example, if your rent today doubled, you might be able to continue paying the same amount of money for all the other stuff ... you will have to cut back spending in other areas

themes.theme: Potential for production-led growth through bank deregulation

arguments.conclusion: Bank deregulation could allow banks to buy treasuries, lower interest rates, and increase lending for production, leading to higher real GDP and lower inflation.
premises: The Fed wants to move away from QE and needs banks to buy treasuries.
Regulatory tweaks can enable banks to buy treasuries freely.
Increased lending for production can bring down prices through production outpacing money supply.
This could lower debt-to-GDP and inflation simultaneously.

evidence.item: Bank deregulation is coming.
evidence.verification_basis: Prediction stated as fact without evidence or timeline.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: bank deregulation is coming

evidence.item: Federal Reserve wants to get away from managing monetary policy via balance sheet and QE.
evidence.verification_basis: Claim about Fed intentions without attribution or supporting statement.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260403_Are We About to See Stagflation in the US.txt
evidence.source_excerpt: Federal Reserve wants to get away from trying to manage monetary policy by manipulating its balance sheet and sending it higher through QE

candidate_matches.text: The Federal Reserve and Treasury are implementing policies (buybacks, deregulation, yield curve control, SLR removal) and the executive branch is attacking Fed independence, all aimed at supporting government borrowing, which will lead to inflation, asset bubbles, and benefit banks at the expense of the public.

The U.S. government's accelerating deficit spending and borrowing will force the Federal Reserve to adopt unconventional monetary policies such as yield curve control or quantitative easing, leading to inflation, a decline in the purchasing power of the dollar, and a wealth transfer from savers to borrowers.

The US economy faces high risk of a severe downturn due to structural weakening in the jobs market and supply shocks like the oil crisis from the Strait of Hormuz closure, which also drives gold crash via liquidity crisis, and investors should prepare with reserve strategies.

Bank deregulation, specifically removing the supplementary leverage ratio, is the most effective solution to prevent a crisis in private credit, reduce stagflation risk, and stimulate economic growth by enabling banks to lend to both the government and the private economy, ultimately benefiting asset owners.
The Federal Reserve is covertly or indirectly engaging in quantitative easing to support government borrowing, which will expand the money supply and prevent a debt crisis but cause inflation.
